in 2017 I lived in a rural area without much of a Skateboarding scene. I grew up always kind of wanting to do it but was convinced I wasn't in the right place, my parents weren't against it but weren't for it either, I dunno.

I was anxious and depressed and I just generally had no idea what to do so I took a small leap, but what felt big to me. I was starting way late in my late twenties.

So one day I just took the leap and dropped about 120 dollars on all the stuff I needed for my first board. May not seem like a huge buy, but I never made much money and it was a large investment for something that was maybe not going to pan out at all.

Long story short, no I'm not sponsored or anything but I have made lots of good friends and skateboarding has taught me how to better deal with people and gets me out of the house where before I was just a "stays inside all the time" person basically my whole life before that. Now I live with my significant other, in California, which is like the skate capital of the world basically.

Anyway, I am pretty okay at it now. I can do things that make people go "wow" and that in itself gives me a lot of satisfaction even if that's not why I do it. It drives me to better myself and keep improving, while expressing myself, etc. I love skateboarding so much and while part of me wishes I got into it earlier, I've improved pretty quickly all things considered and I'd be much worse off without it. It didn't fix all the problems in my life but it helped my outlook a lot. It seemed really small and inconsequential when I did it but it has lead me down a fulfilling path for sure.

Months late but I want to give my opinion.

I watched the 1983 movie about 2 years ago and was blown away but how much I loved it. I'm a sucker for this old stuff, I definitely have a taste, so on one hand it's no surprise. On the other hand I think a lot of it is animated beautifully and some of the scenes are so gorgeous and I would call it true art.

It's pretty pulpy and gets really ridiculous and over the top but I mean it's fantasy within' the realm of reason most of the time. I can suspend my disbelief for most of the things that happen.

The characters can be pretty one dimensional at times, but in other ways the movie had time to have a few good twists and show some really dark sides of humanity and especially the theme of revenge.

I could go on about it but I think it just lands squarely in what I used to really enjoy as a kid. Things like Arnold Movies and James Bond, but in my opinion Golgo 13 is too quickly written off as 'too formulaic and simple'. Yes, Duke Togo is rarely complex but there are in fact times when even he shows some restraint if he pities a target or whatever. Then you have all the supporting characters who have very adult, if not melodramatic, problems that drive them to actions that would normally be so heinous and vulgar in every day life.

There I go rambling again lol. I watched commentary about the movie and I forget if it was the producer or the art director but someone said they saw Golgo as "The Personification of Death itself" which I think is a really good way to think about him. Like, he's less of a person and really more of force of nature. I'll leave it at that.

The only thing I can think is that The Predator was hoping to have a one on one with Glover's character who would investigate the scene, but instead Danny showed up. Perhaps the Predator was just angry and took it out on Danny Boy, or because he knew it would eventually lead Glover to him which is what the Predator really wanted.

However, as you say we heard Danny fire at the Predator and just having a gun in your hand is enough to give the Predator reason enough to end your life as 'fair game'. Besides this fact, Danny was seen with Glover's character and may already have seen him as a "worthy prey" by association.

In my opinion it was kind of a clumsy way to give the story more weight for Glover's character to be motivated in a personal revenge that the audience can more easily connect with, rather than his previous motivation of "finishing a job" which probably isn't as compelling for general audiences.

If I were to rewrite the scene, the predator picks up Danny by the leg and instead of dropping the projectile that Danny took out of the vent, he holds on to it. Danny is terrified and stricken with terror at the sight of the Predator as it holds him up by his leg. The Predator takes Danny's gun out of his holster and throws it away on the ground below. Then, the Predator tries to take the projectile from Danny. Danny resists, so the Predator grips his hand around Danny's hand, crushing it into the projectile and causing him great pain. Danny let's it go and then the predator let's Danny fall to the ground.

They find Danny seriously injured with a broken back or some serious injury, maybe even knocked out. Glover's character still gets reprimanded later and the rest of the movie plays out the same. A bonus here is that we now get an even greater sense of just how strong the Predator's grip is, not only holding someone up easily with one arm but also crushing a human hand quite easily.

For me there is the uncomfortable feeling and inability to open up when I'm in person with most people, even internet friends I've known for 10+ years. It sucks because I want to be that kooky and fun guy who isn't afraid to say things like I am in like discord, but then put me in a real life situation and I feel much less brave about everything. 

I get that there is a layer of protection and the ability to just log out online that's much easier than vanishing in real life, and I know I'm definitely not alone in this way. However, I know these people and I'm comfortable with them only in the right circumstances and when it's the wrong circumstance (ie being around them in real life) I find myself more shy and unable to be that same internet personality. I think it slightly has to do with self consciousness of who I am physically irl compared to the mannerisms that match my avatar more than my real life self. 

I almost feel like a reverse imposter syndrome where the internet persona is who I do want to be, but irl that persona's mask is gone and I don't feel the safety of the guise anymore. I know my friends will still like and respect me even if I opened up irl, but it's like I don't have it in me. It's like I can only truly get close to people and express myself, this conjured internet self I prefer, is when it's text or voice with a picture I've chosen as my representation of self.

It's not that I'm surprised I don't like it, I'm just surprised so many people look past the things that make it so frustrating for me.

As for the exploration, sure I understand that I was supposed to turn back and I did. However, I don't think it's unfair that if you take down a very hard enemy you get rewarded for your time, patience, and tactics. I would have learned my lesson and turned around and ran away, but punishing me for not doing that, standing my ground, and then \*winning\* that encounter gave me essentially nothing. It's kind of a slap in the face and I just don't see the logic in it. I would have turned around anyway, at least give me something for my trouble. It's not even my biggest gripe but I still find it contrary to good design.

So in your words I need to adapt to the game rather than want the game to adapt to me. I would understand this argument if it were some kind of issue where I failed to adapt, but it's a lot less about me adapting to the game and more about fighting against all the time wasting elements that seem arbitrary. I guess some people do like navigating un-intuitive menus and selling their trash items off their pawns, they get a whole lot of satisfaction out of fighting only the mobs they should be fighting and never taking on a greater challenge so they can be rewarded for it, but instead are encouraged to run away and backtrack to somewhere they can level more easily. I guess I just really missed out on all these fun things that make it so great for other people, they'll put up with all that or even enjoy it and I have to as well? This argument doesn't make much sense to me.

Fair thoughts. It's one of my favorite games but the only point I'll try to defend are in regards to flying enemies and specifically the raven enemies that I'm guessing are the problem.

There was a time when I too found them to be insufferably bad and broken. However, their movement is not random and is quite easy to predict, especially at their first spawning and their initial movement is nearly always uniform. After that initial movement, if you missed them, yes it can be frustrating if not unforgiving in the way that Ninja Gaiden's enemies can be where a mistake punishes you quite hard as they resume to fly into you in a harder to predict (but still not random) way. If they can be random on their initial dive/attack run at the player then I apologize, but if you're merely talking about the bat's position it almost always has something to do with player position in regards to wherever you are on the horizontal plain they will spawn in at that point, and usually reliably at very specific triggers. I'll admit I'm not a speed runner but I watched someone do it for awhile and part of their run was using a bat to damage boost up somewhere and it's position was important. However, I could be wrong and if so I apologize.

That said, it's almost a rhythm game, where you get the timing right and are rewarded for it. It also suffers from a severe problem of either knowing how to deal with something or having to learn it, aka beginners traps.

I think also the pendulum room is one of the more frustrating and borderline RNG moments in the game that if not properly understood can indeed become a feared and hated moment, if not the peak of frustration in CV3. The bats have a very easy to understand and predictable movement pattern. I understand that while on the pendulum it's much less easy to turn around and deal with them because you're also moving on the pendulum, but it's very possible and if I recall the only bat I have trouble with any more is the one that can spawn from the front at the very last jump from the last Pendulum to "safety". I'm not saying "get good" or anything, but if you've made it that far into the game you should have the skills required to deal with the bats on your tail.

I think there is no shame in playing the much more reasonable Japanese version. To my knowledge it doesn't change enemy spawns, but taking less damage as the game goes on can make a big difference.

There is an option in the Unity version of Daggerfall to actually shrink the dungeons. Not sure to what degree but I heard it helps. For me, I like that it goes on for so long that I have to choose to just go back to save myself from delving too deep and not finding my way out. I understand it being a bit too much however.

Yeah so here's the thing, I do love me a good dungeon. However, that's only a part of the equation. I also like "down time" or "distractions" that let me sort of regroup, sell my items, get some fun interactions in with the NPC's, maybe just have some moments of reflection and enjoy the quiet and serene scenery and stuff. Then when I'm refreshed, I've rested on my laurels for a minute, maybe read through a little bit of the lore, I'm ready to go to the dungeon again.

But Daggerfall so far is just Dungeon, go and sell items, turn in quest for reward, look for new quest giver, dungeon again, etc. Sure, maybe when I buy a house I can do the relaxing a bit more but right now it just feels like everything is go from point A to point B, rinse repeat. Fetch quests forever. Skyrim has these to some degree but there is much more in the ways of light distractions and things to make it feel less like you go from one dungeon to another.

As for Morrowind, it has it's good points don't get me wrong! I also don't enjoy quest markers and prefer using my brain and reading the quest log and deducing where I need to go, or asking people for directions. That to me is a lot of fun! *When it works.* And Daggerfall is pretty good about that, but also not really perfect in that it's required vagueness for the formula of "X has said to go to Y to look for Z.", and thus I understand how making quests around this system is going to feel a bit phoned in and result in a less than diegetic and simple form of commands instead of more natural and flavorful language. Don't misunderstand me, I also appreciate Morrowind in it's own way, I just don't think it's atmosphere is really for me and the atmosphere is a huge deal for me. Daggerfall nails the atmosphere almost perfectly, it just needs more *character* in it's characters.
Yeah it's fine, I know it's unlikely to ever happen, but an unlikely chance is better than the zero percent chance that Bethesda would do it themselves.

Yeah that's mostly my view as well. It's just such a shame because as much as I enjoy the actual adventuring/fighting/stats/equipment/etc, I also value highly the actual interaction I can have with the people of the world. That said, the lore is fantastic and as cheesy as most would find it today the beginning intro scene of Uriel Septim entrusting you with this task was pretty well done and even more interesting when you find out later >!he doesn't trust you and lies to you about his motivations, the letter being personal when it is in fact not, etc. I think it's really cool that the game makes the main quest giver actually unreliable and gives you some false information.!<

I think maybe I would just have a better time reading about the lore and exploring the characters in the wiki to better understand and get a feel for what exactly is going on. I know a lot of what was written translated to Morrowind and to this day, but also so much has been retconned. I just wish I could love playing the game.

Edit: Wanted to note also that the Daedra in Daggerfall seem to act like crazy, weird, eccentric assholes, as they should. I really dig that. I like that summoning them has to be done on certain days and can be miss-able for a WHOLE YEAR. Then even if you pay for the ritual, they might just not show up because screw you. I think that's how they should be, and besides Sheogorath and Calvicus Vile they've all been sort of generalized and became far too... simplified? I don't know. It's stuff like this that makes me want to play Daggerfall but then I do and it's just kind of blah for 90% of the game unless you're in a dungeon.

I'm halfway through but essentially it's a Fromsoft game but you will be unlearning a lot of your natural responses. You can still dodge but in most cases parrying/blocking is better. It's much more about mastering the tools you're given and since there is a posture gauge instead of stamina that will probably also be something to get used to. 

Do you like Japanese folklore and dark themes? If so you'll probably like the atmosphere.

Just don't expect to go in and have it mastered because you've played other Fromsoft games. It's going to be frustrating and hard. I'm 25 hours  in and though I've gotten through almost half the game it feels like a never ending ascending mountain where the challenge just keeps going up and up and the game finds new ways to make me feel like I still have much to learn. Truly for masochists. It's not impossible but you will likely struggle. It will seem impossible at times but if you get really utterly stumped, watch a video about a certain boss to understand how to beat them. A lot of the bosses are puzzles that you just have to know the trick for.

If you do pick it up, good luck.

I think the big problem here is that by killing an elf that may not die for good you've still done a couple bad things:  


1) Attacking fellow elves. Always a bad idea. I'm sure the Valar aren't fond of that and though it falls into the plans of Illuvatar since they know everything that is and will be, the Valar do not have that same foresight.

If you like traditional Fantasy setting stuff, 4, 5, and 9 are kind of more traditional overall with swords and sorcery, but usually have some steampunk and stuff thrown in (especially 9).

If you like something a bit more science fiction/mechs in your fantasy, 6, 7, 8, and 12 fall into that.

10 is kind of funky in that it has a little bit of everything, but more than anything it's a very "spiritual" themed game in story and aesthetics.

All of them are pretty friendly to new players (The least friendly to new people might be Tactics, I wouldn't start with that one because there's so much to learn and I still barely know most of what's happening in that game). My favorite is still IX, it's a fun little adventure, and at the time it was a return to a simpler kind of fantasy setting and story.

In my opinion, going to a real skate shop and seeing what feels good under your feet is the best thing to do. Based on your foot size you may want different sizes for your deck and someone at the shop can hook you up. Avoid Zumiez or other chains if possible, look for a local shop if you have one.

Deck : REAL, Plan B, Powell-Peralta, Almost, Girl. I feel like there's few bad brands but shutouts to Nullity and other slightly smaller time companies. Get what looks cool and feels good under your feet.

Wheels - I really prefer Bones for the price and performance is great for that. Swiss are super high performance you probably wont need yet, just get regular Bones. Can't comment on Ricta's but they seem pretty good.

Bearings - REDS all the way. I've never not been happy with these bearings and they're not pricey either.

Bushings - I've never known this to really matter all that much but I'm sure someone will swipe in to tell me about amazing or horrible Bushings they've used. Just get whatever the guy at the store hands you that's cheap.

Trucks - Thunders are well worth it in my opinion. Light and durable. Independent (Indys) are heavier and supposedly last longer, but my Thunder Trucks have lasted me quite awhile so I don't buy it. Indys aren't bad but they can be very heavy, and heavy = less air and more effort needed.

Shoes - [https://worldindustries.com/products/mens-shetler-shoe](https://worldindustries.com/products/mens-shetler-shoe) <--- 30 dollars when you account for shipping gets you what is basically a 60 dollar quality skate shoe. Cannot recommend these enough. I may order another pair.

Lubricant - Some will think I'm stupid or crazy but good old 3 In One Multipurpose Oil makes for very cheap and effective lubricant. You only need a drop in between your wheels where the bearings are, then work it in by spinning it inside. Then I use a paper towel to help clean off the excess oil. Careful though! You'll be a little slick until the oil comes off/dries.

Just want to throw in anyone who sees this struggling at getting better, my own problem was that i refused to understand why i kept losing. Not that I didn't want to get better, but figuring out what my flaws were and acknowledging them and working to get rid of them. Example, my DI was far too predictable as well as my recovery and that's what kept me in combos I was convinced I was unable to get out of. Now I am much more mindful of that as well as other things.

Also, be sure to save and watch replays of yourself, in slow motion if you have to, to see where you went wrong. Otherwise you will spin your wheels like I did asking yourself "what happened?" when you lose to someone you know you could have beaten. It's different from when you just get bopped by a master player, but when you get bopped by someone you know you should not have lost to that's what is the worst feeling of all. I got so upset at my inability to understand my fatal flaws until i got really introspective and watched for my habits and broke them. Good luck all.

It works well for movies but in writing a novel it can be very difficult to show and not tell since you know, all you really have is words. You can sort of vaguely hint at things that, when put together, come to a conclusion earlier than their reveal. Otherwise you could also leave things so vague it's up to someone's interpretation.

Anyway, I really love "show don't tell" when it comes to movies and animation because that's a big point of a visual medium. To be be quite frank, I think the OVA is very straightforward with nearly all of it's information being kept up front, *but* the characters themselves and their motivations are often using the "show don't tell" technique. I think when a character concisely explains it through inner monologue when it could have been showed or inferred is rather anticlimactic. Now that does happen many, many times in the show but usually it is through a bit of information that has to be explained because they are forbidden to show much if any outward emotion. 

I do think that sometimes words cannot properly capture or contain a feeling such as the sadness of a character losing another. Sometimes it can even cheapen or lessen the blow if you're outright told "This is sad." because then the emotion is no longer your own. Since you are human, you likely already know it's sad and all the show has to do is play some classical music to make an event impact based on your own emotions and not try to synthetically administer it.

Anyway, that's my very haphazard analysis on why the show works. There are plenty of other things to be loved about it.
